title: Man fatally shot by police had lengthy criminal record:
subtitle: Victim had replica pistol in waistband or on lap when police approached
article: A man with a replica pistol who was fatally shot by two Vancouver police officers Saturday had a lengthy criminal record in Ontario and was wanted for two separate robberies in Burnaby, police said Monday.

Homicide Inspector Chris Beach, who identified the dead man as 46- year-old Thomas Evon Stevenson, said the replica pistol was either in his waistband or on his lap when officers approached him and that he appeared to be reaching for the gun.
"He didn't put his hands in the position that we would have wanted them," Beach said. "The gun was in his waist area and the wounds are consistent with his right arm going across his torso.

"It \[the officers' actions\] was certainly understandable if you were faced with that type of scenario, where you saw a weapon and the right arm there in this manner. One might easily come to the conclusion that that was a threatening gesture."
Beach said an autopsy was to be conducted Monday on Stevenson, who had just arrived in Vancouver from Toronto a week ago.
Vancouver homicide detectives are investigating the death of Stevenson, who was shot in an allegedly stolen car on East Pender Street.

Police said the officers, veterans who each have at least 10 years' experience, were on patrol and were running routine checks on vehicles they passed. Stevenson was sitting in a car -- an older white Toyota Tercel, one witness said -- that had been stolen in Burnaby.
The officers approached the car in the 400-block Pender and spotted what looked like a pistol. Beach said the officers fired several shots after Stevenson appeared to reach for the gun.
The shots were fired through a closed window, but Beach refused to say exactly how many times Stevenson was shot, only that he was hit in the torso.
He said the two officers had had no previous dealings with Stevenson and did not know about his criminal record.
Police said the case will be treated like any other homicide. The information will get passed on for review by Crown counsel, who will decide whether to proceed with any legal proceedings.
Beach said he sees no conflict with the Vancouver police department investigating the matter. "I have every confidence in my investigators. They will determine the truth."
He said the investigation will likely take a couple of months before being forwarded to Crown counsel.

The two officers will take some time off before going back to work, although Beach said he didn't know whether they would return to the street right away. He also said they will receive counselling. "It's very, very traumatic."

Beach said Stevenson had a record for armed robbery in Ontario and at one point was sentenced in Toronto to three-and-a-half years in jail for five robberies in which firearms were used. He didn't know why Stevenson moved to Vancouver.
He also said the officers who shot him thought they were only dealing with a man who had stolen a car. He wouldn't comment when asked if either officer had been involved in previous shootings.
Beach warned against buying replicas designed to look like real guns.

"There are far too many. One of the messages we'd have is that these are not things we'd encourage people to have. I don't know what good comes out of someone having an imitation handgun. I don't know why people would have them."
Vancouver police also said Stevenson was wanted in Burnaby on two robbery counts, but had no particulars other than that the robberies happened recently.
Burnaby RCMP did not return a call asking for details.
Vancouver police Constable Sarah Bloor said investigators are not saying specifically at this time what type of gun the replica resembled, other than it resembled a pistol.
Corrections Canada could not be reached Monday for comment on Stevenson's parole status.
Vancouver coroner Nic Snyckers said Monday an inquest will likely be held into Stevenson's death, but only if Crown counsel decides not to charge the officers involved in the shooting.
Replica handguns have been an continuing problem for police officers who have mistaken them for the real thing.
In February 2000, two police officers had some tense moments when a man aimed a replica handgun at them as they assisted an assault victim outside a Downtown Eastside hotel.

Vancouver Constable Anne Drennan said at the time that while police assisted the victim, a third man not connected to the fight came up and pointed what appeared to be a handgun at the officers. She said the officers were not in a position to draw their own handguns, but managed to overpower him a few moments later.
She said the gun turned out to be a replica, but was "very real looking."
In 1994, a Vancouver teenager came dangerously close to being shot by police after they received a call about a man with a gun in the False Creek area.
With guns drawn, plainclothes officers made the youth surrender his real-looking weapon -- a replica of a chrome-plated Smith & Wesson .45-calibre semi-automatic.
The 15-year-old, who was playing cops and robbers with a 16-year- old friend, thought an officer with a drawn gun was also playing the game.
The teen later told police he almost aimed his gun at the officer, who had his service revolver pointed at the youth.

A man with a replica 9-mm pistol was shot twice in 1993 by a city police officer at Abbott and Hastings. Witnesses said the man, who survived, reached for his gun, tucked in the waist of his pants, after an officer ordered him to keep his hands in the air.
